exactBodyChange.before:
## Chef's Note

Ratatouille comes from Nice in Provence, France, where it's been made since the 18th century as a way to use up summer vegetables. The name comes from the French 'touiller,' meaning to stir or toss food. The Pixar movie made it famous worldwide, though that version shows a tian (sliced vegetables baked in a dish) rather than traditional ratatouille which is more of a rustic stew. The key is cooking each vegetable separately first - eggplant, peppers, and zucchini all have different cooking times and water contents. Roasting at high heat rather than stewing prevents the vegetables from becoming mushy and develops caramelized flavor.

## Directions

1.  **Stage 1 (Roast):** Preheat oven to 425°F. On one sheet pan, toss eggplant with 2 tbsp oil and salt. On another, toss peppers, zucchini, and squash with 1 tbsp oil and salt. Roast for 15-20 minutes until caramelized and tender.
2.  **The Base:** In a large Dutch oven, sauté onion in 2 tbsp oil for 10 minutes until golden. Add garlic for 30 seconds.
3.  **The Sauce:** Stir in the grated tomato pulp. Simmer over medium-low for 15 minutes to reduce the liquid.
4.  **Combine:** Carefully fold the roasted eggplant, peppers, and squash into the tomato sauce. Simmer for 5 minutes to let the flavors meld.
5.  **Finish:** Remove from heat. Stir in the fresh basil, red pepper flakes, and a squeeze of lemon for the mandatory **Acid Balance**.
6.  **Serve:** Serve hot or at room temperature with a final drizzle of high-quality olive oil.
exactBodyChange.after:
## Chef's Note

Roast eggplant separately from the pepper and squash, then add each tray to the tomato sauce when its vegetables are tender. The source finish uses basil, red-pepper flakes, oregano and a measured teaspoon of olive oil. The lemon-finish variation stays separate so every oil and seasoning has one destination.

## Directions

1. **Prepare eggplant tray:** Heat the oven to 425°F with racks in the middle and upper third. Use large rimmed baking sheets, bare or lined with parchment rated for 425°F. Toss eggplant, extra-virgin olive oil, and fine sea salt on one tray, using all its oil and salt, then spread in one layer. Divide among more trays if necessary rather than crowding.
2. **Prepare other vegetables:** Toss large bell pepper, medium-to-large zucchini, large yellow squash, extra-virgin olive oil, and fine sea salt on a separate tray with all its oil and salt. Spread in one layer. Put the eggplant on the middle rack and the other vegetables on the upper rack; roast 15 minutes before the first stir.
3. **Start sauce while trays roast:** In a large Dutch oven or soup pot over medium heat, cook medium yellow onion, extra-virgin olive oil, and fine sea salt using all the base oil and salt, stirring until the onion is tender with some golden edges, about 8–10 minutes.
4. **Add garlic:** Stir cloves of garlic into the onion and cook about 30 seconds until fragrant, lowering heat if it begins to darken.
5. **Simmer tomatoes:** Add ripe tomato, using the full prepared amount, and stir up any browned bits. Reduce heat to maintain a gentle simmer while the trays finish; the sauce should thicken without catching.
6. **Finish trays separately and combine:** After the first 15 minutes, stir each tray and swap rack positions. Begin checking eggplant around 10 minutes later; when tender and golden at the edges, fold it into the simmering tomatoes. Keep the pepper and squash roasting until tender and browned at the edges, often another 5–10 minutes after the eggplant. Fold all the remaining vegetables and their oil into the sauce and simmer together 5 minutes. Check each vegetable rather than treating one roasting clock as universal.
7. **Finish off heat:** Remove from heat and stir extra-virgin olive oil, fresh basil, red pepper flakes, dried oregano, black pepper, fine sea salt, and fresh lemon juice (if using) through the full pot: use all the measured finishing oil, basil, red-pepper flakes and crumbled oregano for the source route, then black pepper and extra salt only to taste. The optional lemon is for the distinct variation below, not an automatic addition to the source finish.
8. **Serve:** Divide the whole pot into the listed portions. At the original batch, the six more-modest portions may instead serve four as generous mains. Use extra-virgin olive oil (if using) and fresh basil (if using) if desired. Serve hot or briefly cooled for room-temperature service; refrigerate promptly if waiting longer.

savedOriginal.directions:
Preheat the oven to 425 degrees Fahrenheit with one rack in the middle of the oven and one in the upper third of the oven. Line two large, rimmed baking sheets with parchment paper for easy clean-up, if desired.

To prepare your tomatoes, remove any woody cores with a paring knife. Then, grate them on the large holes of a box grater into a bowl (this is easiest if you hold the tomato at a diagonal), and chop any remaining tomato skin. Or, blitz the tomatoes in a food processor until they are broken into a frothy pulp. Set aside.

On one baking sheet, toss the diced eggplant with 2 tablespoons of the olive oil until lightly coated. Arrange the eggplant in a single layer across the pan, sprinkle with ¼ teaspoon of the salt, and set aside.

On the other baking sheet, toss the bell pepper, zucchini and yellow squash with 1 tablespoon of olive oil and ¼ teaspoon salt. Arrange the vegetables in a single layer. Place the eggplant pan on the middle rack and the other vegetables on the top rack. Set the timer for 15 minutes.

Meanwhile, warm 2 tablespoons of the olive oil in a large Dutch oven or soup pot over medium heat. Add the onion and ¼ teaspoon salt. Cook, stirring occasionally, until the onion is tender and caramelizing on the edges, about 8 to 10 minutes.

Add the garlic, stir, and cook until fragrant, about 30 seconds. Add the tomatoes, and use a wooden spoon or sturdy silicone spatula to stir any browned bits stuck to the bottom of the pan into the mixture. Reduce the heat to medium-low, or as necessary to maintain a gentle simmer.

Once 15 minutes are up, remove both pans from the oven, stir, and redistribute the contents of each evenly across the pans. This time, place the eggplant on the top rack and other vegetables on the middle rack.

Bake until the eggplant is nice and golden on the edges, about 10 more minutes (the eggplant will be done sooner than the rest). Remove the eggplant from the oven, and carefully stir the eggplant into the simmering tomato sauce.

Let the squash and bell pepper pan continue to bake until the peppers are caramelized, about 5 to 10 more minutes. Then, transfer the contents of the pan into the simmering sauce. Continue simmering for 5 more minutes to give the flavors time to meld.

Remove the pot from the heat. Stir in 1 teaspoon olive oil, the fresh basil and red pepper flakes. Crumble the dried oregano between your fingers as you drop it into the pot. Season to taste with additional salt (I usually add ¼ teaspoon more) and black pepper.

Serve in bowls, perhaps with a little drizzle of olive oil, additional chopped basil, or black pepper on top (all optional). Like all stews, this ratatouille’s flavor improves as it cools. It’s even better reheated the next day. Ratatouille keeps well in the refrigerator, covered, for 4 days, or for several months in the freezer.
